prompt:
A physics student observes a 100 m sprint event at an athletic track meet.
[FIGURE PLACEHOLDER: Schematic diagram of a straight 100 m sprint track showing starting blocks at 0 m and a finish line tape at 100 m, with an electronic timer display indicating a winning time of approximately 12.0 s]
(a) State a reasonable estimate for:
(i) the mass $m$ of a teenage sprinter, with appropriate unit [1]
(ii) the average speed $v$ of the sprinter during a 100 m race completed in about 12 seconds, with appropriate unit [1]
(b) Kinetic energy is calculated using $E_k = \frac{1}{2} m v^2$. Using your estimates from (a), calculate a reasonable estimate for the sprinter's average kinetic energy, showing your working clearly. [2]
(c) Use scale bracketing to evaluate the physical plausibility of the calculated kinetic energy:
(i) Explain why an estimate of $50\text{ J}$ is unphysically low. [1]
(ii) Explain why an estimate of $500\text{ kJ}$ ($500\,000\text{ J}$) is unphysically high. [1]

parts.description: State reasonable sprinter mass with unit
State average sprint speed with unit
Calculate estimated kinetic energy using formula
Explain why 50 J is unphysically low
Explain why 500 kJ is unphysically high

part_enrichment.guidance: Award B1 for mass in range 50 kg to 75 kg with unit kg.
part_enrichment.common_pitfalls: Quoting mass in grams or unphysically large values.

part_enrichment.guidance: Award B1 for speed in range 7.5 m/s to 9.0 m/s (e.g. 100 / 12 = 8.3 m/s) with unit m/s.
part_enrichment.common_pitfalls: Omitting unit or forgetting to divide 100 by 12.

part_enrichment.guidance: Award M1 for substitution into 0.5 x m x v^2, and A1 for calculated value in range 1500 J to 3000 J (e.g. 0.5 x 60 x 8.33^2 approx 2100 J) with unit J.
Award B1 for stating that 50 J is the kinetic energy of a thrown cricket ball or slow bicycle, far too small for a sprinting human.
part_enrichment.common_pitfalls: Giving vague answers without physical comparison.

part_enrichment.guidance: Award B1 for stating that 500 kJ is vehicle kinetic energy, far exceeding human muscular work capacity.

answer:
(a)(i) 60 kg (range 50 to 75 kg)
(a)(ii) 8.3 m/s (range 7.5 to 9.0 m/s)
(b) Ek = 0.5 x 60 x (8.3)^2 approx 2100 J (range 1500 J to 3000 J)
(c)(i) 50 J corresponds to a thrown ball or gentle toss, far smaller than a whole human body sprinting.
(c)(ii) 500 kJ corresponds to the kinetic energy of a fast-moving passenger car, far exceeding what human muscles can generate.

mark_scheme.criterion: (a)(i) States a mass in the range 50 kg to 75 kg with unit kg.
(a)(ii) States an average speed in the range 7.5 m/s to 9.0 m/s (or 100 / 12 = 8.3 m/s) with unit m/s.
(b) Shows substitution into 0.5 x m x v^2 using stated estimates.
(b) Value in the range 1500 J to 3000 J (or 1.5 kJ to 3.0 kJ) with unit J.
(c)(i) Explains that 50 J is the energy of a light projectile / ball, far too small for a running adult.
(c)(ii) Explains that 500 kJ is the kinetic energy of a motor car / requires machinery, far exceeding human physical work output.

hints: In (a)(i), think of teenage body mass.
In (b), square the speed before multiplying by mass and 0.5.
In (c), compare 50 J and 500 kJ to everyday moving objects (a ball vs a car).
solution:
(a)(i) Sprinter mass m approx 60 kg (acceptable range 50 kg to 75 kg).
(a)(ii) Average speed v = distance / time = 100 m / 12 s approx 8.3 m/s (acceptable range 7.5 m/s to 9.0 m/s).
(b) Kinetic energy E_k = 0.5 x m x v^2 = 0.5 x 60 kg x (8.33 m/s)^2 = 0.5 x 60 x 69.4 approx 2080 J approx 2100 J (or 2.1 kJ).
(c)(i) 50 J is the kinetic energy of a 1 kg object moving at 10 m/s (such as a thrown sports ball). A 60 kg human running at 8 m/s has far more moving mass, making 50 J an absurdly low estimate.
(c)(ii) 500 kJ (500 000 J) is the kinetic energy of a 1000 kg car travelling at over 30 m/s (over 100 km/h). Human muscular power cannot generate this level of mechanical kinetic energy in a sprint.
teacher_walkthrough: A hallmark Cambridge physics question linking kinematics and energy estimation.
Notice how parts (a) through (c) build a coherent chain: initial physical benchmarks, formula calculation, and scale bracketing validation.
Ensure students quote realistic values with appropriate units at each stage.

provenance.abstract_pattern: biomechanical parameter estimation, kinetic energy calculation, and bracketing
provenance.independence_statement: Authored as an original multipart question combining human kinematics with kinetic energy bracketing.
